title: Adding winter temperature and precipitation to the spatial benchmark did not close the US bird thermal-tracking gap, and better-fitting niche models did not predict local change (BBS 1966-2025)
abstract: Question: campaign work found that bird community temperature indices (CTI) follow only a small part of the spatial CTI slope on summer temperature. Is this gap an artefact of a one-axis yardstick, given that winters warmed faster than summers and precipitation changed? Data: North American Breeding Bird Survey (3,960 contiguous-US routes, 107,922 runs, 467 species, 1966-2025) with nClimGrid temperature and precipitation; UK Butterfly Monitoring Scheme (1,253 sites, 1976-2024) with E-OBS. Method (plan written before outcomes): cross-fitted species temperature indices; spatial benchmarks of route-mean CTI on May-July temperature alone, plus December-February temperature, plus annual and summer precipitation, and all four axes; expected trend = spatial slopes x route climate trends; observed trend with route and observer fixed effects; block bootstrap (186 BBS draws). For 357 bird species, cross-fitted quadratic niche models with one or four axes predicted route change from 1971-1990 to 2006-2025. Results: the expected BBS CTI trend was 0.093 C per decade with summer temperature and 0.096 with four axes; observed 0.023. Realised fractions were 0.25 (95% CI 0.18-0.37) and 0.24 (0.18-0.35); gap closure -5% (-19% to +2%). Precipitation change added at most 0.016 C per decade. Only summer temperature plus precipitation inside 2-degree blocks closed 29% (10-50%), and this vanished with winter temperature added (1%). The West followed 0.45 and the East 0.19-0.21 with every benchmark. Four-axis niche models fitted space much better (median cross-validated R2 0.28 vs 0.08) but did not predict local change inside 2-degree blocks (transfer -0.01, CI -0.09 to 0.07; one axis -0.02; full transfer 1; prediction reliability 0.96-0.98). Spatial fit did not predict temporal skill (Spearman -0.00). UK butterflies with European indices followed 0.14-0.28 of the four benchmarks, but GB temperature and precipitation are collinear and intervals are wide; UK niche models fitted poorly. Conclusion: the weak thermal tracking of US birds is not caused by a summer-only climate yardstick; the deficit is in the temporal response. Limitations: correlational design; collinear axes; simple additive niche models; start-point climate; no detection model; UK tests have low power.
